note: Showroom feed — every image features real products SDLR installs, and each caption names the selections so followers can DM to get the look. IMAGES: all nine were regenerated 2026-09-30 as brand-new Google Nano Banana Pro images (imagen-nano-banana-2, 4:5) — nothing reused from the library or earlier runs. Each was downloaded and visually checked one by one, realism-passed where photoreal, and every frame shows the neighboring houses around the lot per Gio's 2026-09-28 rule. Job tier is deliberately varied: a flagship Poway estate (Monday), a compact Mission Hills bungalow driveway (Tuesday), a mid coastal Encinitas outdoor room (Wednesday), a mid Carlsbad evening terrace (Thursday), and an attainable Carmel Mountain Ranch suburban yard (Friday) so both entry and estate buyers see themselves. Curb appeal holds its slot: Tuesday is a Mission Hills paver-driveway and front-yard post. Monday is a drone aerial — the first in several weeks — for scale. No neighborhood repeats from the last three weeks. CAROUSEL WEEK: the last process carousel ran Sep 16, so Wednesday Oct 28 is a five-slide process carousel — 2D plan, 3D bones, full 3D design, the built yard at golden hour, the built yard lit at dusk. All five slides show the SAME Encinitas design on a normal lot with two-story neighbors right over the side walls: the full 3D design render (slide 3) was generated first and then passed as a reference image for the plan, the bones and both photoreal built shots, so the layout matches across every slide. Slides 1-3 are deliberately VIP3D / Lumion-style CGI and a hand-rendered plan (clearly a design, not a photo); only slides 4-5 are photoreal and realism-passed — that is the honesty of the format. The plan drawing carries no legible wording of any kind and shows the neighboring lot lines and roof outlines at its edges. The built shots were taken from a lower eye-level camera so they read as photographs, not the render (early attempts that looked like the render were regenerated); the golden-hour slide 4 was generated from both the 3D render and the dusk photo, so slides 4 and 5 show the same single-story house from the same spot, day and night. SEASONAL: Halloween is Saturday Oct 31 and is not a luxury design-build moment, so no Halloween post. Thursday instead uses a real and useful seasonal hook — daylight saving ends Sunday Nov 1, so the yard goes dark by five — to carry the landscape-lighting post. Friday rotates the Trust & Difference angle off 'one contract, one firm' (used the last two weeks) onto the 10-Month Walk-Through, a real SDLR program. Nothing auto-posts. Post natively in the Instagram app; upload the Wednesday slides in numbered order.

posts.alt: Drone aerial of a Poway estate backyard at golden hour: a long rectangular pool with a raised spa and spillway, a silver travertine deck, a SYNLawn Golf putting green with flagsticks, a black louvered pergola over a lounge with a fire table at the corner of the pool deck, olive trees, agave and grasses, a sand-stucco Spanish tile-roof home, and neighboring tile-roof estate homes on the lots all around with more homes across the chaparral hills beyond
posts.hook: From the ground, an estate yard is a series of good ideas. From above, you find out whether they were ever one plan.
posts.caption:
A lot this size doesn't fail on materials. It fails on spacing.

So the whole yard is set on axes before anything is chosen. The pool runs the long axis off the main living wing, so water is what you see from inside the house. The putting green takes the flat run of the lot instead of fighting it. The pergola lounge anchors the corner where the pool deck meets the green, so it looks out over both without sitting in the middle of either. Everything planted stays low, olive and agave and grasses, so the hills stay in the picture.

An acre doesn't make a yard feel generous. Spacing does.

The selections:
• silver travertine pool deck & coping
• raised spa with spillway
• SYNLawn Golf putting green
• StruXure louvered pergola
• mature olive trees, agave & ornamental grasses

Sitting on a big lot and not sure where anything belongs? DM “DESIGN”.

posts.alt: A 1920s Spanish Colonial bungalow in Mission Hills at golden hour with white stucco, a clay tile roof and arched windows, a Belgard herringbone paver driveway and front walk edged in a charcoal soldier course, a raised dark stacked-stone planter filled with agave and blue senecio, clipped hedges, path lights, a lantern-lit entry porch, a blooming jacaranda street tree, and neighboring craftsman bungalows right next door on both sides
posts.hook: A 1920s Spanish bungalow deserves better than a strip of gray concrete.
posts.caption:
Old Mission Hills homes were built with real craft at the front door. Then somebody poured a driveway in 1978, and it has been the loudest thing on the lot ever since.

This one gives the house its manners back. The field is Belgard pavers in a tight herringbone — the pattern interlocks under car weight and reads as brickwork rather than paving, which is the right register for a house this age. A charcoal soldier course edges the whole run and the walkway, so the driveway has a drawn line instead of a ragged edge against the planting. The raised Eldorado Stone planter lifts the agave and succulents to eye level as you come up the walk, and low path lights carry you to the door after dark.

Same footprint the house has had for a hundred years. It just finally matches it.

The selections:
• Belgard herringbone paver driveway
• charcoal soldier-course border
• Eldorado Stone veneer planter wall
• agave, blue senecio & succulents
• FX Luminaire path & entry lighting

posts.alt: Five-slide SDLR process carousel of one Encinitas outdoor living space on a lot with two-story neighboring homes right over the side walls: a hand-rendered overhead plan showing the neighboring lots, the hardscape bones modeled in 3D, the full 3D design with pergola, kitchen, turf and planting, the finished build photographed at golden hour, and the finished build lit at dusk
posts.hook: You should know exactly what your backyard looks like long before anyone breaks ground.
posts.caption:
Most people meet their backyard for the first time on the day it is finished. That is a strange way to spend that kind of money.

Swipe through one outdoor living space, drawing to done:

1. The plan — every edge, bed and tree placed overhead first.
2. The bones in 3D — paving, seat walls, the fire trough, the kitchen volume, the pergola frame. No planting yet, because the structure has to be right on its own.
3. The full design — pergola, kitchen, turf, planting. This is the model you walk through and change until it is actually yours.
4. Then we build it.
5. Then we light it, because that is when you will really use it.

Slides one through three are the design. Four and five are the build. The whole point is that they match.

The selections:
• silver travertine terrace with charcoal border
• StruXure louvered pergola
• Lynx built-in grill & raised bar counter
• Warming Trends linear fire trough
• board-formed concrete seat walls
• SYNLawn turf panel · FX Luminaire lighting

Want to see your own yard in 3D before you commit to anything? DM “DESIGN”.

posts.alt: A Carlsbad backyard at dusk with landscape lighting on: warm uplights in two olive trees and a tall palm, recessed step lights in travertine steps, a glowing strip under a board-formed concrete seat wall, a round fire table burning between two cream lounge chairs on a grey paver terrace, agave and rosemary beds, a white board-and-batten farmhouse with a dark metal roof lit from within, and neighboring two-story stucco homes just over the side fences
posts.hook: The clocks go back Sunday. By next week your yard is dark at five.
posts.caption:
For the next four months, most of the hours you are actually home, that yard is a black rectangle behind the glass.

Lighting is what buys those hours back — and it is layers, not floodlights. Warm uplights inside the olive canopies so the trees become the ceiling of the room. Step lights so a grade change is obvious without anyone having to look down. A low wash under the seat wall so the terrace reads as though it is floating. The fire does the rest, and the space stays genuinely usable on a fifty-eight-degree Tuesday in January.

It is the most living space you will ever add to a house without moving a wall. And it only exists after dark.

The selections:
• FX Luminaire low-voltage lighting
• Techo-Bloc Blu 60 paver terrace
• Warming Trends CrossFire fire table
• board-formed concrete seat wall
• olive trees, agave & rosemary

Want the yard to still be there after five? DM “DESIGN”.

posts.hook: We come back ten months later and go looking for everything wrong with it.
posts.caption:
For most contractors the last day on your property is the day they get paid. That is the part we do differently.

Ten months after we hand a project over, we come back and walk it with you. No charge, nothing to sign. Ten months is the honest interval: the yard has been through a winter of rain and a full summer of heat, the base has settled, the planting has filled in, and the joints have moved if they were ever going to. Anything that was going to surface has surfaced by then. We would rather find it ourselves than have you living with it and being too polite to call.

That is what standing behind the work looks like when it is not a slogan.

The selections:
• Belgard Mega-Arbel paver patio
• SYNLawn turf panel with paver banding
• Bull built-in grill, Eldorado Stone veneer island
• Warming Trends gas fire pit
• Kichler path lighting

Want a firm that is still around in month ten? DM “DESIGN”.
